promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 6 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: Last week's 53 miles and 20-miler show real fitness, but that was a 43 percent jump in one week and too big to repeat. This week drops back to about 38 miles with an easy 14-mile long run so your legs can absorb it.

answers.question: I ran way more than the plan and felt fine. Can I keep this up?
answers.answer:
No, not at this level, and not by adding miles on top of the plan. You went from 37 to 53 miles in one week. A jump that size often shows up as a niggle one to three weeks later. Feeling fine right now is common after a jump like this, and it does not mean your legs have absorbed it.

Your right knee flared in August, in a week of about 32 miles, so the risk is real for you. This week comes back to about 38 miles. After that the plan builds into the mid-40s, with long runs capped near 18 miles. That is enough for your goal, and it gets you to the start line healthy.

new.analysis:
**Last week was strong running, but it was not the week that was planned.** Every run went longer than planned, Monday's rest day became a run, and Wednesday got a fourth rep. The table shows where the extra 15 miles came from.

| Day | Planned | Ran |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mon Sep 7 | rest | 4 mi easy |
| Tue Sep 8 | 6 mi easy | 7 mi easy |
| Wed Sep 9 | 8 mi, 3 x 1.5 mi at 8:00/mi | 9 mi, 4 x 1.5 mi at 7:55/mi |
| Thu Sep 10 | 5 mi easy | 7 mi easy |
| Fri Sep 11 | rest | rest |
| Sat Sep 12 | 4 mi easy | 6 mi easy |
| Sun Sep 13 | 15 mi, heart rate under 150 | 20 mi, average 149, drifting to 153 |
| Total | 38 mi | 53 mi |

**The fitness behind it is real.** Your easy runs held 139 bpm at about 9:50/mi, the same as before the August heat. The threshold reps held 7:55/mi with no fade, and the 20-miler had even splits all the way through.

**The risk comes from the size of the jump, not from how it felt.** Mileage rose about 43 percent in one week, and the long run grew by 6 miles. Heart and lungs adapt to that faster than legs do, so feeling fine now does not mean the load has been absorbed.

**Sunday was a steady run, not an easy long run.** Your heart rate started near 146 and drifted up to 153, so 88 percent of the run was above your easy zone. That one run is why only 54 percent of the week was easy running, against a target of 80 percent.

**It also went past the three-hour limit I use for your long runs.** After about three hours, extra time on your feet adds more wear than fitness. At your easy pace, three hours is about 18 miles, so you never need to go further than that.

**This week goes back to roughly what last week was meant to be.** That makes the 53 a one-off rather than your new normal. It also gives your calves and right knee a quieter week. Keeping one threshold session means your fitness keeps moving while the overall load comes down.

**The rest of the block has room to build again.** From the week of Sep 21, Tuesday grows into a medium-long run and the long runs build to about 18 miles. One of them will include miles at marathon pace, about 8:35/mi, before the taper starts in mid-October.

**You do not need another 20-miler to run under 3:45.** In your Sep 2 session you ran the marathon-pace miles at 8:34/mi, and they felt like effort 6/10. That is right on goal pace. From here, the job is to reach the start line healthy with that fitness intact.

settingsProposalBullets: In mid-August the outside of your right knee hurt on downhills during a long run. It settled within a week with hip and glute work.
You often add miles when you feel good or when you run with your club.
Your easy runs sit around 9:50/mi at 139 bpm, and your easy-day heart rate limit is about 145.
You do strength work twice a week.
Hot weather pushes your easy-run heart rate up by about 12 bpm.

safetyCallouts.title: Get the calves checked if the tightness lingers.
safetyCallouts.body: Tightness after a 20-miler is common, but if it turns into pain, gets worse from day to day or changes how you walk, stop running and see a physio.
